title: The Exposure Window: Patching Against a Public Exploit
subtitle: A fleet of servers, one vulnerability, and the race between the patch rollout and the attackers who start scanning the day an exploit is published.
lead: A vulnerability is disclosed and a fix ships the same day. Nothing is exploited yet, so the fix waits for testing and then for the next ((maintenance window)). Somewhere along the way a working ((exploit)) is published, scanning starts, and every server that is still unpatched becomes a target.

This page runs that race day by day for a fleet of a thousand servers. The rules count how many servers are still unpatched, how many of those are exposed, and how many ((host-day))s of exposure pile up, then turn that into expected compromises. Values are ((expected value))s and the numbers are illustrative. Scroll: the cards and pinned chapters move the clock for you, and the dock lets you play it yourself.

parameters.label: Unmanaged long tail
parameters.description: Servers no patch process reaches: forgotten test boxes, appliances, shadow IT.

parameters.label: Fast track once exploited
parameters.description: Out-of-cycle emergency patching as soon as an exploit is public.

parameters.label: Virtual patch
parameters.description: A filtering rule in front of the servers that blocks most exploit attempts until they are patched.

parameters.label: Daily chance an exposed server falls

rules.label: Scanning picks up
rules.note: From the day the exploit is out, attackers add scanners until they reach full speed.

rules.label: Has testing finished?
rules.note: The fix ships on day 0 and needs the testing time before any rollout.

rules.expr: patchable * max(if(maintenance && ready, windowShare, 0), if(fastNow, fastShare, 0))
rules.label: Patch in a window or on the fast track
rules.note: A window patches its share of the reachable servers at once; the fast track patches its pace every day.

Unpatched and reachable by the exploit

rules.note: One exposed server for one day is one host-day.

events.label: Exploit published
events.note: A working exploit appears in public; scanning starts.

events.label: Maintenance window
events.note: The regular window in which changes are allowed.

scenarios.label: Monthly cycle
scenarios.description: Test for a week, then wait for the monthly window. The exploit appears on day 14.

scenarios.label: Fast track
scenarios.description: The same cycle, but once the exploit is public, patch a quarter of what is left every day.

scenarios.label: Shield first
scenarios.description: Monthly cycle with a virtual patch in front of the fleet from day 2.

scenarios.label: Late exploit
scenarios.description: Monthly cycle, but the exploit only appears on day 45.

sections.title: Two clocks start on disclosure day
body: On day 0 the vulnerability is public and the fix is out. One clock is yours: testing, then the next maintenance window. The other belongs to attackers: the day a working exploit appears, after which scanning ramps up over {rampDays|duration}.

What matters is not when you patch, but how many servers are still unpatched while the exploit is public, and for how long. That product is the **exposure**, counted in ((host-day))s. Right now it stands at **{exposureDays}**, and the expected compromises at **{compromised}**.

figures.title: Both clocks
figures.caption: The red marker is the exploit; blue markers are maintenance windows.

steps.title: Monthly cycle
steps.text: Test for a week, wait for the window on day 30. The exploit lands on day 14, in the gap: **{compromised}** expected compromises after four months.

steps.title: Fast track
steps.text: Emergency patching starts the day the exploit is public: **{compromised}** expected compromises, mostly from the long tail.

steps.title: Shield first
steps.text: A virtual patch from day 2 blocks most attempts until the window: **{compromised}**.

steps.title: Late exploit
steps.text: The exploit only appears on day 45, after the first window: **{compromised}**.

sections.title: The patch pipeline: test, wait, roll out
body: The fix is ready after {testDays|duration} of testing. From then on, every maintenance window patches **{windowShare}** of the servers a rollout can reach. Servers in the ((long tail)) are never reached: {unmanaged} of the fleet that nobody remembers to patch.
The step line shows the unpatched count dropping in stairs, one stair per window. The table shows today's arithmetic, rule by rule.

steps.title: Day 0: the fix ships
steps.text: Every server is still unpatched: **{unpatched}**. The fix is out, but it has to be tested first.

steps.title: Day 7: tested, and waiting
steps.text: Testing is done; nothing moves, because no maintenance window has come yet. Watch the flow: the rule that patches has nothing to do.

steps.title: Day 30: the window
steps.text: The window patches **{patchedToday}** servers in one day. The pulses run from what is reachable to what is patched.

steps.title: Day 60: the second window
steps.text: Another window, another stair. What is left now is mostly the long tail: **{longTail}** servers no rollout reaches.

sections.title: Once the exploit is out, every unpatched server counts
body: On day {exploitDay} the exploit is published. Scanning starts slowly and reaches full speed after {rampDays|duration}; at full speed an exposed server falls with a daily chance of {hitRate}. This chapter is pinned: keep scrolling and the clock runs through the first two months of the monthly cycle.

figures.title: Exposed servers
figures.caption: The area is the exposure: servers times days.

check.prompt: With the monthly cycle, how many servers are still exposed on day 29, the day before the first window?

options.text: None: the fix was ready on day 7
options.why: Ready is not deployed. Without a window or a fast track, a tested fix changes nothing.

options.text: About half: some teams patch early
options.why: Only if someone patches outside the window; in this model nobody does.
Every server waits for the window on day 30, so all of them are exposed from day 14 to day 29.

check.reveal: On day 29, **{exposed}** servers are exposed and the exposure has reached **{exposureDays}**.

marks.text: Day 0. Disclosure and fix on the same day. No exploit yet, so nothing is exposed.
Day 7. The fix is tested and ready, and it waits for the window.
Day 14. The exploit is published. Every one of **{unpatched}** servers is exposed at once.
Day 24. Scanning is at full speed. Exposure so far: **{exposureDays}**.
Day 30. The window finally patches most of the fleet; **{exposed}** servers stay exposed.
Day 45. The rest of the story is the long tail: **{compromised}** expected compromises and counting.

sections.title: Patch faster, shield first, or hope the exploit is late
body: Three ways out. The **fast track** starts emergency patching the moment the exploit is public. **Shield first** puts a ((virtual patch)) in front of the fleet on day {mitigationDay}, so most exploit attempts fail until the window. And sometimes the exploit is simply **late**, and the monthly cycle looks fine without trying.
The small multiples put the expected compromises of all four scenarios on one scale; the heat map shows exposed servers over time, darker for more.

check.prompt: Which strategy ends the four months with the fewest expected compromises?

options.why: It closes the gap within days, but the long tail stays exposed for the rest of the period, and that adds up.
The shield blocks nine attempts in ten from day 2 for every server, including the long tail that no window ever reaches.
The first window patches most of the fleet before the exploit exists, but the long tail is exposed from day 45 to the end.

check.reveal: In this scenario the expected compromises are **{compromised}**. Switch scenarios to compare.

steps.title: Fast track
steps.text: Once the exploit is public, a quarter of what is left is patched every day. The gap closes within a week.

steps.title: Shield first
steps.text: The virtual patch covers **{covered}** servers today; only **{exposed}** are really exposed.

steps.title: Late exploit
steps.text: On day 30 there is nothing to exploit yet. Day 45 is a different story.

sections.title: The servers nobody patches decide the end of the story
body: Whatever the patching strategy, the long tail stays unpatched long after the windows have done their work; only a shield covers it. After the first month it is most of the remaining exposure, as the weekly bars show.
This is the bench: every knob and the clock. Shrink the long tail, switch on the fast track or the shield, and press play.

glossary.definition: Working code or instructions that use a vulnerability to break into a system. Once public, anyone can run it.
A recurring slot in which changes such as patches are allowed to production systems.
One server exposed for one day. A thousand servers for two weeks is fourteen thousand host-days.
The servers no regular process reaches: forgotten test machines, appliances, systems nobody owns.
A filtering rule in front of a system, for example in a web application firewall, that blocks attempts to exploit a vulnerability until the real fix is installed.
The average outcome over many runs; 2.5 expected compromises means two or three on a typical run.

closing.heading: What the two clocks showed
body: Exposure is unpatched servers multiplied by the days an exploit is public. A regular cycle keeps the first factor high until its window; the exploit date, which you do not control, sets when the second starts.
Fast tracks and virtual patches shorten the gap after the exploit appears; finding the long tail shrinks what is left afterwards. Both count.
takeaways: A tested fix that waits for a window protects nothing.
Exposure is counted in host-days: servers times days.
A fast track turns weeks of exposure into days.
A virtual patch cuts exposure at once but never to zero.
The long tail dominates exposure after the first month.
